description: Three-panel composite figure of age-hardening curves for austenitic Fe-Mn-Al-C steels, built from hardness measurements and tensile tests. (a) Brinell Hardness (y axis, 150-450) versus Aging time (x axis, logarithmic, ticks WQ, 0.1, 1, 10, 100, 1000 h) for Fe-30Mn-8Al-1C-0.35Si [120], with four curves labelled 600 °C, 550 °C, 500 °C and 450 °C; the highest-temperature curve rises first and peaks at the lowest hardness, whereas the 450 °C curve rises most slowly and is still climbing at 1000 h - peak hardness increases as the aging temperature decreases. (b) Same axes for six alloys aged at 550 °C: Fe-30Mn-7.8Al-1.3C [118] reaches the highest hardness (peak near 30 h, just below the 420 gridline, then falls), followed by Fe-34Mn-11Al-0.98C, Fe-30Mn-8Al-1C and Fe-31Mn-7.8Al-0.88C; Fe-29Mn-4.9Al-0.98C and Fe-34Mn-7.1Al-0.5C stay almost flat near 165-190, i.e. no age hardening. (c) Dual-axis tensile data: left Strength (MPa, 400-1600), right TE (%, 0-40), x as in (a); open squares = UTS, filled triangles = YS, filled diamonds = TE for Fe-30Mn-8.5Al-2.0C 550 °C [78], Fe-28Mn-9Al-1.8C 450 °C [77] and Fe-30Mn-7.8Al-1.3C 550 °C [118]. Together the panels argue that higher C content and lower aging temperature raise the peak strength and slow the aging kinetics, with strength and elongation dropping after peak aging.

subfigures.description: Brinell Hardness (150-450) versus logarithmic Aging time (WQ, 0.1, 1, 10, 100, 1000 h) for Fe-30Mn-8Al-1C-0.35Si [120]; four curves labelled 600 °C, 550 °C, 500 °C, 450 °C. Curves start near 165-175 and rise to plateaus/peaks; the fastest-rising curve is the 600 °C one and the slowest (450 °C) is still rising at 1000 h near the 400 gridline.

Brinell Hardness (150-450) versus logarithmic Aging time (WQ to 1000 h) for six alloys aged at 550 °C, labelled with arrows: Fe-30Mn-7.8Al-1.3C [118], Fe-34Mn-11Al-0.98C [120], Fe-30Mn-8Al-1C [120], Fe-31Mn-7.8Al-0.88C [120], Fe-29Mn-4.9Al-0.98C [120], Fe-34Mn-7.1Al-0.5C [120]. Two alloys remain flat near 165-190 (no hardening); the others rise to ~330-410.

Tensile properties versus logarithmic Aging time (WQ to 1000 h), dual y axes: Strength (MPa, 400-1600) left and TE (%, 0-40) right. Legend: open squares = UTS, filled triangles = YS, filled red diamonds = TE. Curves labelled Fe-30Mn-8.5Al-2.0C 550 °C [78], Fe-28Mn-9Al-1.8C 450 °C [77], Fe-30Mn-7.8Al-1.3C 550 °C [118], the latter lying lowest with near-flat UTS/YS.

observations.observation: Panel (a) plots Brinell Hardness (y axis, ticked 150 to 450) against aging time on a logarithmic x axis whose first tick is labelled WQ (water quenched) and which runs through 0.1, 1, 10, 100 to 1000 h; the plotted alloy is labelled Fe-30Mn-8Al-1C-0.35Si [120].

In panel (a) the four labelled curves start at essentially the same value near the 175 gridline and separate with aging time; the curve labelled 450 °C shows the slowest rise and is still increasing at 1000 h, approaching the 400 gridline, i.e. peak hardness increases as the aging temperature decreases.
The citing text states that the Fe-Mn-Al-C alloys in Fig. 31a follow classic age hardening trends and that the peak hardness increases for longer times at lower aging temperatures.
Panel (b) shows six labelled Fe-Mn-Al-C alloys aged at 550 °C, each with an arrow from the alloy label to its hardness curve; all curves begin between about 165 and 215 on the Brinell Hardness axis.

In panel (b) the two lowest curves, labelled Fe-29Mn-4.9Al-0.98C [120] and Fe-34Mn-7.1Al-0.5C [120], remain almost flat across the whole time range near the 165-190 gridlines, showing no age hardening response.
In panel (b) the alloy Fe-30Mn-7.8Al-1.3C [118] attains the highest hardness, peaking at roughly 30 h just below the 420 gridline before decreasing toward 370 at 100 h.
Panel (b) labels one alloy 'Fe-34Mn-7.1Al-0.5C [120]', whereas the citing text refers to the same non-hardening alloy as 'Fe-34Mn-7.8Al-0.5C'; the figure label reads 7.1Al.

The caption states that the aging curves in (a) and (b) were established by hardness measurements, that the (b) data are extracted from Refs. [118,120] and converted to Brinell hardness for comparison, and that (b) shows the effect of the Al and C contents.
Panel (c) uses two y axes: Strength (MPa) on the left, ticked 400 to 1600, and TE (%) on the right, ticked 0 to 40, against the same logarithmic Aging time axis (WQ to 1000 h) as panels (a) and (b).

The legend in panel (c) assigns open squares to UTS, filled triangles to YS and filled diamonds to TE; the three strength curves are labelled Fe-30Mn-8.5Al-2.0C 550 °C [78], Fe-28Mn-9Al-1.8C 450 °C [77] and Fe-30Mn-7.8Al-1.3C 550 °C [118].

In panel (c) the Fe-28Mn-9Al-1.8C alloy aged at 450 °C reaches the highest UTS of the three, peaking just below the 1600 MPa gridline after about 10 h, while Fe-30Mn-8.5Al-2.0C aged at 550 °C peaks earlier (about 3-4 h) at a lower strength near the 1400 MPa gridline, and Fe-30Mn-7.8Al-1.3C aged at 550 °C stays lowest, its UTS rising only to about the 1100 MPa gridline.

The citing text states that the peak strength of the Fe-30Mn-8.5Al-2C alloy appears after 3-4 h at 550 °C while that of Fe-28Mn-9Al-1.8C appears after 10 h at 450 °C, and that the peak strength of Fe-30Mn-7.8Al-1.3C at 550 °C appears after about 20 h.
The citing text states that the increment of peak strength is about 350 MPa when the C content is increased from 1.3% to 1.8%.
The citing text states that increasing Al from 7 to 11% increases the age hardening effect but has less influence on the age hardening kinetics, as seen in Fig. 31b.

The citing text attributes the drop of strength and ductility after the peak aging time in panel (c) to the formation of coarse intergranular κ-carbides, grain-boundary lamellar colonies of discontinuously coarsened κ-carbides, transformed α-ferrite and/or β-Mn precipitates at the γ/γ grain boundaries.
The caption states that panel (c) shows the tensile properties of several alloys as a function of aging time, illustrating the effect of the C content and temperature.

unreadable_items: panel (a): no leader lines connect the temperature labels 600 °C, 550 °C, 500 °C and 450 °C to individual curves, so the exact curve-to-temperature assignment is partly ambiguous
panel (c): the TE (%) points are not labelled with numeric values, so elongation values can only be read approximately against the right-hand axis
